fatal_errors: The hypothesis substitutes a homogeneous single-phase equiatomic FCC alloy for the target as-cast FCC+B2 eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, eliminating the phase-boundary mechanism central to the observed behavior.
It does not reconstruct the controlled 600°C versus 750°C aging comparison or predict the target non-monotonic ductile-brittle-ductile transition.
The proposed nano-twinning/lattice-strain mechanism omits L12 ordering, increased antiphase-boundary energy, planar slip, jagged B2/FCC phase boundaries, and ductile phase-boundary transition zones.

The intervention is underspecified and confounded: heat treatment or composition adjustment is assumed to reduce lattice-strain heterogeneity and nano-twinning without independently controlling grain size, stacking-fault energy, precipitation, or phase stability.
The falsification rule incorrectly treats failure of the intervention to alter the proposed mediator as falsification of the mechanism rather than failure of the manipulation.
explanation: The response addresses the broad question of toughness in FCC high-entropy alloys and offers measurable mechanical and microscopy outcomes, so it is a testable alternative at a general level. However, it does not reconstruct the target material, aging window, structural mediators, mechanism, or non-monotonic outcome. E1 supports deformation nano-twinning in CrCoNi at room-to-cryogenic temperatures, and E3 supports lattice-strain-induced dislocation behavior and strength-ductility synergy, but neither establishes that annealing-induced suppression of these features controls toughness across temperatures up to 800°C. E2 actually highlights intermediate-temperature ductility loss but is not incorporated into a mechanism capable of explaining the target recovery at 750°C. The proposed broad temperature boundary is therefore weakly supported, and the experiment would require direct verification of phase stability, grain size, stacking-fault energy, and other heat-treatment effects to discriminate the claimed mechanism.
